scope: Post-extraction grouping over three existing workflows and registered sources; not new full-paper extraction.

arms.discovery: Unmodified cohort selector, at most six cuts across three complete workflows; then unmodified curation/review/admission.
arms.fixed_boundaries: Four supplied single-operation cuts; unmodified curation/review/admission, no supplied definitions or links.

independent_followup.reason: Joint curation succeeded in the fixed-boundary arm. Test a distinct integration requirement: independent compilers starting with an empty shared registry. Added after observing the joint-arm result; exploratory follow-up, not preregistered as part of the original two arms.

definition.context_requirements: Requires RNA input, anchored oligo-dT priming, template-switch RT, common-handle cDNA PCR and bead recovery within the selected transformation. RT/polymerase brands, TSO sequence/modification, cycle recipe, cell versus total-RNA input and volumes are implementation properties, not separate concept identities.
definition.information_effect: Transfers a poly(A)-selected transcript representation to amplified cDNA with common amplification handles and potential transcript-length coverage, including the association of template switching with RNA 5′ ends. It does not guarantee complete capture of every transcript, preserve RNA strand/original-molecule identity, or create UMIs/cell barcodes from primer anchoring bases.
definition.name: Poly(A)-primed template-switch cDNA preamplification and recovery
definition.operation: Route one input alternative without implying a physical mixing reaction; prime/denature RNA with anchored oligo-dT; reverse transcribe with a template-switch oligonucleotide; amplify the resulting common-handle cDNA by PCR; recover preamplified cDNA by bead purification.
definition.output: Purified preamplified cDNA representing the selected RNA input, before downstream fragmentation, sequencing-adapter construction and sample indexing.
definition.physical_mechanism: At the ordered composite transformation level: anchored oligo-dT directs poly(A)-RNA priming; reverse transcription with a template-switch oligonucleotide forms cDNA suitable for common-handle PCR; thermocycled DNA polymerization preamplifies the cDNA; bead binding/separation and elution recover it. Input-alternative routing is a logical interface, not an extra reaction. Exact terminal covalent intermediates and bead-kit internals are unspecified.
definition.purpose: Generate a preamplified transcript-derived DNA substrate for library construction while preserving the priming/template-switch architecture needed for comparison with other RNA-conversion routes.
definition.substrate: One RNA-containing specimen input, such as an individual-cell lysate or a separately supplied total-RNA input; alternative inputs retain distinct tube/specimen attribution.

concepts.scope_note: Composite shared_mechanism claim at the ordered RNA-to-preamplified-cDNA level, covering input routing, priming, RT/template switching, PCR and bead recovery; not a claim based only on reverse transcriptase. Common-handle inference is marked in member evidence. A useful singleton for comparing transcript capture/preamplification with downstream DNA-library construction, without requiring one RT brand, TSO modification, reconciled single-cell volume or complete end chemistry.

definition.context_requirements: Requires an explicit analytical-qPCR-to-production-cycle decision, distinct analytical/retained production routes, production PCR and recovery within the unit. Fixed-cycle PCR, final qPCR quantitation alone and QC without an amplification controller are insufficient. Brands, input amounts, cycle formula and size selection are per-use properties.
definition.information_effect: Analytical fluorescence information causally determines production cycle count. PCR increases copies while potentially changing representation; recovery determines which amplified fragments reach the output. No return of analytical product, absolute original-molecule calibration or universal optimality is implied.
definition.mechanism_unknown_reason: Shared purpose is analytically informed production amplification followed by library recovery. No common whole-unit mechanism or numerical control algorithm is asserted: initial amplification/split positions, cycle rules, nick-translation evidence and recovery/size-selection mechanisms differ. Known qPCR/PCR submechanisms are not scientifically unknown.
definition.name: qPCR-guided library amplification and recovery
definition.operation: Separate an analytical aliquot from retained production material, use analytical qPCR to determine production amplification cycles, apply that decision to production PCR, and recover the amplified library using the actual cleanup/size-selection route. Preserve the separate analytical material branch and any excluded fractions.
definition.output: A recovered amplified production sequencing library, a separate analytical qPCR product and its readout/cycle-count decision; size-discard fractions occur only where the member performs size selection.
definition.purpose: Recover an amplified sequencing library whose production cycle count is informed by a separate analytical aliquot, retaining the consequences of its recovery route.
definition.substrate: An already adapter-tagged DNA substrate from one specimen lineage, supplied as purified DNA or an explicitly permitted unpurified reaction, including any within-unit initial production amplification.

concepts.scope_note: Whole-unit shared-purpose abstraction from already tagged DNA through analytical branching, qPCR-informed production amplification and library recovery. Initial production cycles before aliquoting are permitted but not required. No common numerical controller or cleanup mechanism is claimed. ATAC stop-before-saturation monitoring and ChIPmentation rounded-up-Cq enrichment remain different implementations; deliberate preservation versus exclusion of long fragments is an explicit comparison property.

definition.context_requirements: Requires actual tagmentation within the selected unit and retention of its adapter-bearing DNA output. Prior tagmentation outside the selection, PCR alone or RNA-to-cDNA synthesis alone is insufficient. No universal brand, cell count, bead support, fixation state, amplification status or exact adapter-end structure is required.
definition.information_effect: Creates a sequencing-adapter-bearing fragment representation of input DNA. Accessibility, antibody-target enrichment or transcript-derived representation follows the member-specific substrate and selection actions; these biological meanings are not interchangeable. Tagmentation, amplification and size recovery may alter representation without preserving original-molecule counts.
definition.mechanism_unknown_reason: This is a shared-purpose claim over the whole input-to-library-material transformation. Tagmentation is a named common substep, but does not establish a common mechanism for cell lysis, affinity capture, crosslink reversal, purification and PCR. Individual mechanisms may be known; no common whole-unit mechanism is asserted.
definition.name: Tagmentation-based DNA library preparation
definition.operation: Prepare or select the substrate as required by its input, perform fragmentation coupled to sequencing-adapter introduction by tagmentation within the selected unit, and retain the resulting DNA library material. Include the actual preparation, capture, washes, release/purification and any indexing/amplification in that whole transformation; these components are not assumed shared.
definition.output: Recovered specimen-attributed DNA fragments bearing sequencing-adapter sequences introduced during this unit. The endpoint may be unamplified DNA awaiting purification/PCR or a cleaned amplified indexed library; readiness, purity and index status remain properties of each use.
definition.purpose: Generate DNA library material by coupled fragmentation and sequencing-adapter tagging, enabling comparison of how biological inputs become sequencing representations.
definition.substrate: A specimen-attributed DNA-containing input: cells/native chromatin, prepared chromatin, or preamplified cDNA. Entry material and prior selection history are properties of each use.

concepts.scope_note: Whole-unit functional abstraction, relation shared_purpose. Required: DNA-containing input, within-unit fragmentation-coupled sequencing-adapter tagging, retained tagged-DNA output and specimen/representation context. Native-accessibility selection, antibody capture, support, deproteinization, purification and optional PCR/index completion are per-use actions/properties, not implied common mechanisms. Output need not be sequencing-ready. This does not establish assay equivalence, substitution, ancestry or a full recipe.

fields.rationale: The query accepts DNA accessible to an adapter-loaded transposome; the target accepts a DNA-containing enzymatic reaction mixture whose DNA is to be retained for subsequent library construction. A mixture containing accessible DNA can meet both input descriptions. The query does not require an enzymatic reaction mixture awaiting recovery, and the target does not require transposome-accessible DNA, so neither substrate scope contains the other.

The query requires one coupled reaction that fragments DNA and introduces sequencing-adapter sequences. The target requires purification and recovery of DNA from a reaction mixture. Producing tagged fragments and recovering an existing DNA fraction are distinct required transformations; neither operation substitutes for the other.

The query asserts adapter-loaded transposase/transposome-mediated transposition coupling fragmentation to adapter-sequence transfer. The target has a null mechanism and explicitly disclaims a common separation mechanism. Its physical mechanism is therefore insufficiently specified to establish mechanistic equivalence, containment, overlap or difference; no cleanup mechanism can be inferred from its purpose or kit reference.

The query ends with an adapter-tagged fragmented-DNA reaction product before separate cleanup or amplification, with proteins or bead association allowed to remain. The target ends with a retained purified DNA fraction for a subsequent library step. Even if the recovered fraction contains previously tagged fragments, the pre-cleanup reaction product and the recovered purified fraction are different selected endpoints.

The query converts sampled DNA into adapter-tagged fragment precursors and allows fragment endpoints and spans to carry context-dependent information. The target transfers existing DNA sequence and any existing adapter information into a retained fraction without an intended new sequence-encoding step, while leaving recovery and size bias unspecified. Shared retention of DNA sequence does not equate the asserted introduction of tags and fragment structure with recovery of existing information.

The query aims to generate sequencing-library precursors through coupled fragmentation and adapter tagging. The target aims to recover DNA from a completed reaction in a usable form for subsequent library construction. Their common downstream library-construction setting does not make these specific purposes equivalent or establish a broader/narrower relationship.

The query requires evidence of actual coupled transposome-mediated fragmentation and adapter tagging, and rejects reagent presence or mere purification of already tagged DNA as sufficient. The target requires actual DNA purification/recovery and rejects direct crude-reaction transfer. Each requires a different executed transformation, while treating input provenance and implementation details as contextual. Their stated whole-transformation boundaries separate the selected tagmentation reaction from the cleanup step.

The query selects the entire tagmentation incubation from DNA input to adapter-tagged fragments and explicitly excludes downstream washes, purification and amplification. The target selects reaction-mixture cleanup to retained purified DNA and explicitly separates earlier transposition and subsequent PCR. The query allows varied tagmentation inputs and interpretations, whereas the target generalizes cleanup across origins and implementations; these generalizations retain different boundaries and endpoints.

The query declares shared_mechanism, grounded in its asserted reaction-level transposition mechanism. The target declares shared_purpose and explicitly makes no common physical separation-mechanism assertion. These are different asserted bases for grouping transformations; the labels do not establish equivalence or scope containment.

The query specifies DNA-containing cells/chromatin or preamplified cDNA, whereas the target specifies an RNA-containing specimen such as cell lysate or total RNA. Both retain specimen attribution, but the definitions do not establish whether any permitted entry preparation satisfies both substrate descriptions, or whether either input class contains the other.

The query requires substrate preparation/selection followed by fragmentation-coupled adapter introduction through tagmentation within the selected unit. The target instead requires oligo-dT priming, template-switch reverse transcription, common-handle cDNA PCR and bead recovery, ending before downstream fragmentation and sequencing-adapter construction. These are distinct whole transformations despite possible PCR or purification substeps.

The query leaves the whole-unit physical mechanism unasserted; naming tagmentation does not supply the missing composite mechanism. The target asserts an ordered priming, template-switch RT, PCR and bead-recovery mechanism. An absent assertion cannot establish equivalence, inclusion or incompatibility with that asserted mechanism.

The query retains DNA fragments bearing sequencing-adapter sequences introduced during the unit, with amplification and readiness variable. The target produces purified preamplified cDNA explicitly before downstream fragmentation, sequencing-adapter construction and indexing. Amplified DNA alone does not make these endpoint states equivalent.

The query creates a sequencing-adapter-bearing fragment representation of input DNA, with biological meaning determined by member-specific selection. The target transfers a poly(A)-selected RNA representation into common-handle amplified cDNA with the stated template-switch/5-prime association. Shared amplification bias or failure to preserve original-molecule counts does not equate those complete information changes.

The query aims to generate DNA library material through coupled fragmentation and sequencing-adapter tagging. The target aims to generate a preamplified transcript-derived substrate for subsequent library construction while retaining the RNA-priming/template-switch architecture. Their purposes concern distinct stages and required outcomes.

The query requires actual within-unit tagmentation and retained tagged DNA, and explicitly rejects RNA-to-cDNA synthesis alone as sufficient. The target requires RNA input, anchored oligo-dT priming, template-switch RT, common-handle PCR and bead recovery within its RNA-to-cDNA unit. Those mandatory actions and unit boundaries differ; relaxed brand or recipe constraints do not remove the distinction.

The query scopes a whole DNA-input-to-tagged-library-material functional abstraction, with selection and finishing actions varying by use and no common whole mechanism asserted. The target scopes an ordered RNA-to-preamplified-cDNA composite mechanism, ending upstream of library fragmentation/tagging. Neither scope describes the other whole selected transformation.
The query declares shared_purpose, whereas the target declares shared_mechanism. These assert different kinds of commonality; neither label implies the other.

The query requires already adapter-tagged DNA in a purified preparation or permitted unpurified reaction; the target requires an RNA-containing specimen before its cDNA-conversion unit. The text does not specify whether any complete preparation qualifies for both entry descriptions or establish a subset relation. Specimen attribution alone cannot resolve that ambiguity.

The query branches an already tagged substrate into analytical and retained production material, uses qPCR to choose production cycles, then performs production PCR and recovery. The target instead converts RNA through oligo-dT priming and template-switch RT, then preamplifies and bead-purifies cDNA. PCR and recovery are shared substeps, but neither operation asserts the other full sequence or analytical controller.

The query explicitly withholds a common whole-unit mechanism and numerical controller, despite acknowledging known qPCR/PCR submechanisms. The target supplies a composite priming, template-switch RT, PCR and bead-recovery mechanism. The missing query mechanism prevents a supported scope comparison with the target mechanism.

The query outputs an amplified production sequencing library plus a separate analytical qPCR product and readout/cycle decision, with discarded fractions where applicable. The target outputs purified preamplified cDNA before downstream fragmentation, sequencing-adapter construction and indexing. Both the library-construction state and the required analytical branch distinguish the endpoints.

The query requires analytical fluorescence information to control production cycle count, followed by copying and recovery of an existing library representation without returning analytical product. The target transfers poly(A)-selected transcript information into amplified common-handle cDNA with the stated template-switch association. Possible PCR-induced representation changes do not equate these whole information effects.

The query seeks recovery of an amplified sequencing library whose production cycles are informed by a separate analytical aliquot. The target seeks a preamplified transcript-derived DNA substrate for later library construction using a specified RNA-conversion architecture. Generic amplification and eventual sequencing do not make these purposes the same.

The query mandates a separate analytical-qPCR-to-production-cycle decision, production PCR and recovery; fixed-cycle PCR or quantitation/QC alone is insufficient. The target mandates RNA input, anchored oligo-dT priming, template-switch RT, common-handle cDNA PCR and bead recovery. Its RNA-to-cDNA unit does not assert the already-tagged-library controller required by the query.

The query covers the whole already-tagged-DNA-to-recovered-library unit, preserving analytical branching, cycle control and recovery consequences without asserting a common controller or cleanup mechanism. The target covers the ordered RNA-to-preamplified-cDNA unit as a shared composite mechanism. Their entry points, defining intermediate actions, endpoints and kinds of abstraction differ.

The query declares shared_purpose and the target declares shared_mechanism. These are distinct assertions about what is shared across members, even though both definitions contain amplification and recovery.

Both require specimen-attributed DNA, but the query specifically starts with already adapter-tagged DNA as purified material or a permitted unpurified reaction. The target names cells/native chromatin, prepared chromatin or preamplified cDNA without resolving prior adapter status. The text does not establish which complete entry preparations satisfy both descriptions or whether either permitted input class contains the other.

The query starts after adapter tagging and performs analytical branching, qPCR-guided production amplification and recovery. The target must include fragmentation-coupled adapter introduction through tagmentation, together with the actual preparation/selection and finishing actions in that larger unit. Optional amplification in the target does not equate its whole operation with the query downstream amplification/recovery unit.

Both physical_mechanism values are null, and both explanations explicitly withhold a common whole-unit mechanism while allowing known member/substep mechanisms. This is the same absence of a whole-unit mechanism assertion, not a claim that their physical processes or substeps share a mechanism.

The material endpoints overlap in recovered amplified sequencing libraries: the target explicitly permits a cleaned amplified indexed library, while the query requires an amplified production library. Neither complete output description contains the other: the query additionally requires the separate analytical qPCR product/readout/decision, while the target requires adapters introduced during the selected unit and also permits unamplified material. The shared material endpoint does not establish equivalence of the whole transformations.

The query requires fluorescence information to determine production cycle count and then copies/recovers an already tagged representation, with a separate analytical branch. The target requires creation of a newly adapter-tagged fragment representation, whose biological meaning depends on its input and selection actions. Potential amplification or size-recovery bias is a shared consequence, not the same complete information transformation.

The query aims to recover an amplified library using production cycles informed by a separate analytical aliquot. The target aims to generate library material through coupled fragmentation and adapter tagging. A common eventual library use does not equate these specifically asserted purposes or make one a broader formulation of the other.

The query requires distinct analytical/production routes, qPCR-based cycle control, production PCR and recovery starting from tagged DNA. The target requires actual tagmentation within the selected unit and explicitly says prior tagmentation outside that unit or PCR alone is insufficient. Thus the query downstream unit does not satisfy the target boundary requirement, and tagmentation alone does not satisfy the query controller requirements.

The query scopes a whole unit from already tagged DNA through analytical branching and controlled production amplification to recovery. The target scopes an input-to-tagged-library-material unit that includes actual tagmentation and its preparation/selection actions, with PCR and finishing optional. An amplification segment that may occur within the target is not the same selected whole transformation as the query.
Both records declare shared_purpose. This compares only the asserted kind of commonality; it does not make their particular purposes, mechanisms or transformation boundaries equivalent.

Both scopes permit a DNA reaction product accessible to an adapter-loaded transposase. The query requires a DNA-bearing reaction mixture containing products for retention but does not require transposase accessibility. The target requires accessible DNA and includes native-chromatin DNA without requiring a prior reaction-product mixture. Neither substrate scope contains the other.

The query recovers DNA already present in a reaction mixture in purified form. The target fragments DNA and integrates sequencing-adapter payloads in the same transposition step. Recovery does not assert either of those changes, and fragmentation with tagging does not assert purification; these are distinct selected actions.

The query explicitly leaves a common purification mechanism unasserted; its explanation identifies a reporting limit rather than a particular mechanism. The target asserts transposase-mediated fragmentation coupled to integration of preloaded adapters. The absent query mechanism cannot establish equivalence, difference, or scope containment relative to that mechanism.

Purified DNA fragments carrying integrated sequencing-adapter payloads and retained for downstream processing satisfy both output descriptions. The query requires purified retained DNA but leaves product type and adapter status open. The target requires fragments with integrated adapter payloads but does not require purification. Each output description therefore permits cases the other does not; a compatible endpoint alone does not equate the transformations.

The query asserts transfer of existing sequence and attached-tag information with recovered molecules, leaving losses and representation changes implementation-dependent. The target asserts creation of adapter-tagged fragments carrying sequence and fragment-span information, with an additional accessibility interpretation only in the stated native-chromatin context. Transfer through recovery and the asserted creation of tagged fragments are distinct information effects, despite their shared reference to sequence and tags.

The query aims to recover existing reaction products in a form suitable for subsequent molecular processing. The target aims to generate adapter-tagged fragments for library construction, with accessibility measurement in native-chromatin uses. Their downstream processing context is compatible, but the stated recovery purpose and fragment-generation purpose are distinct.

The query requires a DNA-containing reaction product, an explicit purification/recovery operation, and retained DNA output; it leaves method, kit, support, downstream use, recovery behavior, and size-selection intent to each use. The target requires accessible DNA and an active adapter-loaded transposase performing both fragmentation and tagging, with enzyme, payload, conditions, and accessibility evidence left to each use. Each specifies a different mandatory selected action, and neither set of requirements establishes the other.

The query groups recovery of existing DNA by shared purpose, asserts no common purification mechanism, and excludes direct transfer, upstream cell/nucleus preparation, and selected actions that only generate or tag DNA. The target groups coupled fragmentation and adapter integration by a transposase mechanism and explicitly says separate purification, adapter ligation, and amplification do not satisfy the transformation. These boundaries distinguish the selected transformations even though both leave implementation details open and disclaim experimental substitution or a complete recipe.

The query declares shared_purpose, grouping DNA recovery uses without asserting a common mechanism. The target declares shared_mechanism, grouping uses that perform the specified transposase-coupled fragmentation and adapter integration. These are different asserted grouping relations, with no equivalence or containment established by the labels.

The query takes DNA templates for sequencing-library construction, including preamplified cDNA; the target takes a DNA-bearing reaction mixture containing products to recover. A DNA reaction product used as a library template can meet both descriptions. The query does not require a prior reaction-product mixture, and the target does not require a sequencing-library template role, so neither substrate scope contains the other.

The query selects the coupled generation of DNA fragments and addition of adapter sequences, ending before separate cleanup or PCR. The target selects recovery of existing DNA products in purified form. Generating and tagging fragments does not perform the purification action required by the target.

The query asserts simultaneous fragmentation and fragment-end adapter addition by a DNA transposome. The target deliberately asserts no purification mechanism and explains that it groups recovery by purpose. With one mechanism unasserted, neither equivalence nor a mechanistic inclusion or difference can be established; a purification mechanism must not be inferred from the named implementation.

The query endpoint is the fragmented, adapter-tagged DNA reaction before separate purification and library PCR. The target endpoint is recovered, purified DNA retained for another step. These are different material states at different selected endpoints, even when purification could follow tagmentation in a workflow.

The query changes template representation by fragmentation and adds adapter-derived access to PCR and sequencing. The target transfers sequence and any already attached tags with recovered DNA, leaving recovery losses and representation changes implementation-dependent. Preserving existing information through recovery is a different asserted change from creating tagged subfragments.

The query aims to create fragments with adapter-derived access for downstream library amplification. The target aims to recover DNA from a reaction mixture for further molecular processing. Their possible participation in the same workflow does not equate these purposes.

The query requires DNA and evidence of coupled transposome fragmentation and tagging within the selected reaction. The target requires a DNA-containing reaction product, an explicit purification/recovery operation and retained DNA output. The query ends before separate cleanup, so its required selected action does not satisfy the target recovery requirement.

The query requires both fragmentation and fragment-end tagging and excludes cleanup alone, separate ligation and indexing PCR alone. The target requires recovery of DNA already present as purified material and expressly excludes selected actions that only generate or tag DNA. These boundaries distinguish the whole transformations rather than alternative implementations of one transformation.

The query declares shared_mechanism, grouping by the coupled fragmentation/tagging mechanism. The target declares shared_purpose, grouping DNA recovery without a common mechanism assertion. These are different declared grouping criteria.

The query permits DNA library templates across origins and amplification histories, explicitly including preamplified cDNA, without a Tn5-specific input condition. The target requires DNA accessible to a Tn5 tagmentation reagent, whether purified or retained in chromatin. The query does not impose that reagent-specific compatibility restriction; the target chromatin and support examples do not themselves exclude other DNA origins.

Both select a single coupled fragmentation and sequencing-adapter-tagging reaction producing tagged fragments before downstream processing. The target additionally requires that Tn5 perform the reaction. The query specifies transposome-mediated tagmentation without restricting its identity to Tn5, so its operation is not limited to the target named-enzyme case.

The query asserts reaction-level DNA-transposome fragmentation coupled to adapter addition at fragment ends, without specifying the transposome identity. The target restricts the same coupled tagmentation-level mechanism to Tn5 transposase. Neither asserts exact oligonucleotide sequences or a complete covalent intermediate; the explicit Tn5 restriction makes the query mechanism class broader at this stated level.

Both endpoints are DNA fragments bearing introduced adapter tags from the selected tagmentation reaction, before downstream purification and amplification. The target permits retained chromatin or support and separates repair and release as well; the query does not require their absence or select those later transformations. Neither endpoint is the completed indexed sequencing library.

The query describes conversion of DNA templates generally into adapter-tagged subfragments accessible to PCR and sequencing, explicitly including the fragment representation of amplified cDNA. The target frames this effect as tagging genomic DNA fragments, with the genomic population determined by input and prior enrichment. The query permits that genomic case as well as its explicitly described cDNA case, without requiring a genomic-only information description.

Both aim to generate fragmented, adapter-tagged DNA for subsequent sequencing-library processing. The query expresses this as adapter-derived access for amplification; the target also explicitly describes downstream library amplification and sequencing in its information effect. The target one-reaction wording describes the same coupled preparation aim, rather than an additional purpose that requires enrichment or a finished library.

Both require DNA and coupled fragmentation plus adapter introduction within the selected unit. The target specifically requires accessibility to Tn5 and reaction conditions supporting its activity. The query requires a DNA transposome reaction without a Tn5 identity restriction and leaves DNA origin, amplification history and implementation conditions to each use. Chromatin association, support and enrichment are not universal target requirements.

Both select the complete fragmentation/tagging reaction and exclude fragmentation alone, separate ligation and downstream amplification alone. The target confines this scope to one Tn5 reaction; the query does not confine the transposome to Tn5. The query pre-cleanup endpoint and the target separation of downstream repair, release and purification are compatible reaction boundaries, while the target enzyme requirement remains narrower.
Both records declare shared_mechanism. This is equivalence of the declared grouping criterion only; it does not remove the target Tn5 restriction or establish equivalence of the full definitions.

Both permit DNA substrates, and the query preamplified-cDNA example and target native-chromatin example are inclusions rather than exclusive input lists. The target expressly requires accessibility to an adapter-loaded transposase, whereas the query calls its input DNA library templates for a transposome reaction. The supplied text does not establish whether these admissibility conditions are equivalent or strictly nested; the different examples alone cannot settle their scope.

Both assert fragmentation and adapter tagging in one selected reaction. The query expressly requires adapter addition to resulting fragment ends and a pre-cleanup/PCR endpoint; the target expressly requires payload integration during the same transposition step. The target does not state the fragment-end placement, and the query does not expressly state payload integration during transposition. Without supplying that molecular correspondence, equality or either containment of the complete operations is unestablished.

The query asserts simultaneous DNA fragmentation and adapter addition to fragment ends by a DNA transposome. The target asserts fragmentation coupled to integration of a preloaded adapter payload by transposase during transposition. The supplied definitions do not explicitly equate the query transposome assertion with that loading/integration requirement or locate the target integration at the query fragment ends. Their shared coupled action alone is insufficient to establish full mechanistic equivalence or a directional inclusion.

As an output assertion, the query requires a reaction containing fragmented, adapter-tagged DNA before separate purification and library PCR. The target requires fragments tagged specifically with integrated sequencing-adapter payloads for downstream processing. The target product meets the generic tagged-fragment output description, while the query output field does not require that integrated-payload status. This output inclusion does not resolve the separately uncertain operation and mechanism comparisons.

Both describe an adapter-tagged fragment representation. A genomic tagged-fragment case with PCR access and fragment-span information can satisfy both accounts. The query additionally permits its explicitly described cDNA representation and requires PCR/sequencing access; the target describes genomic sequence and fragment-span information, with conditional accessibility encoding, without requiring the query PCR-access assertion. These complete information descriptions therefore overlap without either containing the other.

The query specifically aims to create adapter-derived access for downstream sequencing-library amplification. The target aims more generally to generate adapter-tagged fragments for sequencing-library construction and adds accessibility measurement conditionally for native-chromatin uses. The target purpose does not require amplification as the downstream aim, so the query amplification-directed purpose is a narrower case of its library-construction purpose.

The query requires DNA and evidence of coupled transposome-mediated fragmentation and tagging. The target requires an active transposase preloaded with sequencing adapters that performs both actions. Both leave implementation conditions to each use, but the text does not establish whether the query transposome requirement already entails the target loading requirement or whether an additional restriction is being introduced. A strict inclusion or equivalence cannot be assigned from these requirements alone.

Both exclude separate adapter ligation, purification and amplification as satisfying the selected whole transformation, and both allow DNA-origin or state variation. The query additionally emphasizes fragment-end tagging and the pre-cleanup reaction endpoint; the target requires integration of a sequencing-adapter payload by an adapter-loaded transposase. The supplied scope statements do not resolve whether these molecular requirements coincide or have different boundaries. Shared exclusions and the DNA tagmentation alias are insufficient to establish equivalence or containment.
Both records declare shared_mechanism. The identical relation label states the same grouping criterion, while leaving the scope and molecular-requirement uncertainties in the other fields unresolved.

Both permit purified DNA and DNA retained in chromatin. In the substrate dimension, QUERY specifically requires accessibility to a Tn5 reagent, whereas TARGET leaves transposase identity as a use property. This identifies a Tn5-specific input restriction; it does not establish equivalence of reagent loading or tagging chemistry.

Both select a coupled DNA-fragmentation and adapter-tagging event, and QUERY specifically requires Tn5. TARGET additionally specifies integration of sequencing-adapter payloads in the same transposition step. QUERY describes introduction of tags within one tagmentation reaction without specifying that integration step, so the complete operational scopes cannot be ordered from the supplied assertions alone.

QUERY asserts Tn5-mediated coupling of fragmentation and adapter tagging while explicitly limiting its claim about strand chemistry and covalent intermediates. TARGET asserts fragmentation coupled to integration of a preloaded adapter payload during transposition. Tn5 specificity alone does not establish that QUERY asserts the loading and integration mechanism required by TARGET; no missing chemistry is inferred.

At the stated endpoint, QUERY requires DNA fragments bearing introduced sequencing-adapter tags without requiring an integrated-payload structure. TARGET specifically requires fragments tagged with integrated adapter payloads. Integrated payloads satisfy the more general tagged-fragment description, while that description alone does not require integration. QUERY permits retained chromatin or support, which TARGET does not exclude; both leave subsequent library processing downstream.

Both assert creation of adapter-tagged genomic DNA material. TARGET additionally asserts fragment-span information and possible accessibility information in an appropriate native-chromatin context. QUERY instead states that the tagged genomic population depends on input and upstream enrichment and that this operation does not perform that enrichment. QUERY does not resolve the fragment-span or accessibility assertions, and TARGET does not make accessibility universal, so neither equivalence nor a directional information-effect scope is established.

Both aim to produce fragmented, adapter-tagged DNA for sequencing-library construction. TARGET describes accessibility measurement as a native-chromatin use, with its scope note leaving accessibility interpretation as a use property. QUERY neither requires nor excludes that library application, so it does not impose a different purpose boundary.

Both require accessible DNA and coupled fragmentation plus sequencing-adapter tagging, while leaving substrate state, supports, reagent brands and reaction conditions to individual uses. QUERY specifically requires Tn5; TARGET allows enzyme identity to vary but expressly requires an active adapter-loaded transposase. QUERY does not clearly state the latter loading requirement. These texts do not establish containment of the complete requirement sets, and the omitted loading condition is not treated as an affirmative alternative mechanism.

Both select the coupled fragmentation/tagging unit and exclude separate ligation, purification and amplification as substitutes for that unit; neither asserts a complete recipe or experimental substitution. QUERY selects one Tn5 incubation and leaves exact strand chemistry outside its assertion. TARGET selects fragmentation and adapter-payload integration by an adapter-loaded transposase of unspecified identity. The Tn5 restriction is clear, but whether the complete QUERY unit necessarily satisfies TARGET loading and integration boundaries is not established, so the whole scopes cannot be declared equivalent or ordered.

Both records explicitly use shared_mechanism as their relation category. Equality of this category does not establish equivalence of their selected transformations or their detailed mechanism assertions.

A DNA-bearing reaction mixture can contain DNA accessible to Tn5, so an input may satisfy both descriptions. QUERY also permits accessible purified or chromatin-associated DNA without requiring a prior DNA reaction product. TARGET requires a DNA-bearing reaction mixture containing products to retain, but does not require those products to be Tn5-accessible. Neither substrate description contains the other.

QUERY fragments DNA and introduces sequencing-adapter tags in one Tn5 reaction. TARGET recovers DNA already present in a reaction mixture in purified form. QUERY places purification outside its selected transformation, and TARGET excludes selected actions that only generate or tag DNA. These are distinct complete selected actions despite their possible occurrence in one workflow.

QUERY asserts a Tn5-mediated coupled fragmentation/tagging mechanism. TARGET has a null physical_mechanism and expressly groups recovery by purpose without asserting a common purification mechanism; its kit-reporting limit is not a claim that individual mechanisms are scientifically unknown. There is no TARGET mechanism assertion to compare for identity, difference or containment.

QUERY requires fragments bearing newly introduced sequencing-adapter tags but does not require purified material. TARGET requires purified DNA reaction products but leaves adapter status and product type as use properties. Purified adapter-tagged DNA fragments fit both endpoint descriptions; QUERY also allows material still associated with chromatin or support, and TARGET also allows DNA products without the tags required by QUERY. This shared possible endpoint does not make the transformations equivalent.

QUERY adds sequencing-adapter sequence tags to genomic DNA fragments. TARGET transfers existing sequence and any existing attached-tag information with recovered DNA, with losses or representation changes left implementation-dependent. Addition of tags and recovery of pre-existing information are different asserted effects; recovering tagged DNA does not itself assert the tag-creation effect.

QUERY converts input DNA into fragmented, adapter-tagged material for sequencing-library preparation. TARGET recovers existing DNA products from a reaction mixture for subsequent molecular processing. A shared downstream workflow does not equate generating tagged fragments with recovering existing products.

QUERY requires accessible DNA and a selected Tn5 unit performing both fragmentation and adapter introduction. TARGET requires an existing DNA-containing reaction product, an explicit purification/recovery operation and retained DNA output. Neither an active Tn5 tagging reaction nor purification alone satisfies the other selected unit, even when both operations occur consecutively in the same experimental context.

QUERY covers the complete coupled Tn5 incubation from accessible DNA to tagged fragments and assigns repair, release, purification and amplification to separate transformations. TARGET covers recovery of DNA already present as purified material, excludes simple direct transfer and selected actions that only generate or tag DNA, and asserts no common recovery mechanism. Their selected actions and boundaries differ rather than defining broader and narrower versions of one whole transformation.

QUERY is categorized as shared_mechanism, whereas TARGET is categorized as shared_purpose and explicitly declines to assert a common purification mechanism. These are different stated abstraction categories.
